TCP/IND/4005 · CRVA future hazard · district level

Where each Rama Rao hazard bites

Two questions guide this page. Is climate getting worse here? looks at each district against its own past. Where should we act first? ranks districts against each other. Below the aggregate, each of the 15 future-hazard indicators from Rama Rao et al. (2020) is mapped by district from the INDRA-CMIP6 14-model ensemble (baseline 1985–2014). Colours are oriented so that red is always worse for agriculture and blue better. Outlined districts are hotspots, identified either as the worst 10% of districts (percentile) or as districts more than one standard deviation worse than the mean change across districts (SD). Either way a district only counts if its change is actually adverse.

Aggregate future hazard

Rainfall rule. More rain counts as better only where the district's 1985–2014 rainfall is below 1,500 mm; in wetter districts an increase is neutral. Less rain counts as worse everywhere.
Weights. Atlas Table 5c weights, with unusually hot days, unusually cold days and drought set to 0 because the ensemble-mean data cannot represent them. Their 20% is shared among the other 12 in proportion.

Districts at least 10% worse than their historical mean

For each district, the change in the indicator relative to its own 1985–2014 mean, (future − historical) / historical. A district counts when that relative change is 10% or more in the harmful direction: a fall for rainfall and rainy days, a rise for the other indicators. Districts whose historical mean is zero have no relative change and are left out of that indicator's count.

Method. Each value is the district mean of the 0.1° INDRA-CMIP6 ensemble over the future window minus the 1985–2014 baseline (percent change for rainfall and rainy days). Unusually hot and cold days use ±2 standard deviations of the baseline daily anomaly instead of the Atlas's ±4 °C, and drought proneness is proxied by SPI-3 drought frequency, because averaging 14 models removes most day-to-day and year-to-year variability. Windows: ~2050 = 2036–2065, ~2100 = 2071–2100. Hotspots: the percentile method flags the worst 10% of districts; the SD method flags districts whose change is more than one standard deviation worse than the mean change across all districts in that scenario. No values are removed; map colours saturate beyond the 2nd and 98th percentiles for readability only.

Source: Rama Rao C.A. et al. (2020), Atlas on Risk and Vulnerability of Indian Agriculture to Climate Change, ICAR-CRIDA, Tables 1 and 5c and section 4.4.
